##### **1.8 Generalization of the Simplex Framework and Starting Solution Prerequisites** The **simplex algorithm** generalizes to any linear program by decoupling the direction of optimization (maximization versus minimization) from the geometric requirement of maintaining feasibility across iterations. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6.5 flowchart TD A["Formulation constraints
and right-hand sides"] --> B{"All constraints ≤
and b ≥ 0?"} B -->|Yes| C["Origin Feasible:
Initialize with slack basis"] B -->|No| D["Origin Infeasible:
Artificial variables (Big-M / Two-Phase)"] C --> E["Check Optimality Condition
Max: nonbasic coeff < 0
Min: nonbasic coeff > 0"] D --> E E -->|Condition Met| F["Current Tableau Optimal"] E -->|Condition Not Met| G["Select Entering Variable
Apply Feasibility Condition
Min ratio test with a_ir > 0"] G --> H["Gauss-Jordan Pivot
Update Tableau Basis"] H --> E ``` ###### **1.8.1 Unified Simplex Optimality Condition** The **simplex optimality condition** governs the selection of the entering variable to ensure a monotonic improvement in the objective value $z$: * **Maximization:** The entering variable is the nonbasic variable possessing the *most negative* coefficient in the objective ($z$) row. The algorithm reaches optimality when all coefficients in the $z$-row are nonnegative ($\ge 0$). * **Minimization:** The entering variable is the nonbasic variable possessing the *most positive* coefficient in the objective ($z$) row. The algorithm reaches optimality when all coefficients in the $z$-row are nonpositive ($\le 0$). When an objective row contains no candidate variable with the required sign, the current basic feasible solution cannot be improved, certifying global optimality. ###### **1.8.2 Universal Simplex Feasibility Condition** The **simplex feasibility condition** identifies the leaving variable through the **minimum ratio test**. Given an entering variable index $r$ with constraint coefficients $a_{ir}$ and current basic solution values $b_i$, the leaving variable index $l$ is chosen by: $$\frac{b_l}{a_{lr}} = \min_{i} \left\{ \frac{b_i}{a_{ir}} \;\middle|\; a_{ir} > 0 \right\}$$ This condition applies identically to both maximization and minimization problems. Restricting candidate denominators strictly to positive values ($a_{ir} > 0$) ensures that the new basic variable increases along the extreme edge of the polyhedral cone without violating the nonnegativity bounds ($x_j \ge 0$) of the remaining basic variables. Negative coefficients ($a_{ir} < 0$) and zero coefficients ($a_{ir} = 0$) are ignored because they impose no upper bound on the increase of the entering variable. ###### **1.8.3 Prerequisites for Natural Origin Feasibility** Standard simplex tableau construction assumes the algorithm initiates at the geometric origin: $$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \dots & x_n \end{bmatrix}^T = \mathbf{0}$$ This starting basis is naturally feasible if and only if the system satisfies two structural conditions: 1. Every functional constraint is an inequality of the less-than-or-equal-to type ($\le$). 2. Every constraint right-hand side is non-negative ($b_i \ge 0$ for all $i = 1, \dots, m$). Under these conditions, introducing non-negative slack variables $s_i \ge 0$ converts the inequalities into equations of the form $\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j + s_i = b_i$. Setting all original decision variables to zero yields: $$s_i = b_i \ge 0 \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$$ The slack variables provide an immediate $m \times m$ identity matrix $I_m$ embedded within the constraint coefficient matrix, serving as the starting basic feasible solution. ###### **1.8.4 Breakdown of Origin Initialization and Artificial Starting Solutions** When a linear program contains greater-than-or-equal-to constraints ($\ge$) or equality constraints ($=$), setting $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ yields an infeasible starting point. For a constraint $\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j \ge b_i$ with $b_i > 0$, conversion to standard equality form requires subtracting a non-negative **surplus variable** (or negative slack) $e_i \ge 0$: $$\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j - e_i = b_i$$ Evaluating this equation at the origin $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ forces $-e_i = b_i \implies e_i = -b_i < 0$, which violates the nonnegativity restriction $e_i \ge 0$. Furthermore, an equality constraint $\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j = b_i$ contains neither a slack nor a surplus variable, providing no column vector to populate an initial identity basis. To initialize problems where the natural origin is infeasible, an **artificial starting solution** is constructed by introducing non-negative **artificial variables** ($R_i \ge 0$) into each constraint lacking a starting basic variable: $$\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j - e_i + R_i = b_i \quad \text{or} \quad \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j + R_i = b_i$$ These artificial variables provide an initial identity basis $I_m$, allowing tableau pivoting to begin. Because artificial variables have no physical or economic meaning in the original model, they must be driven to zero by the algorithm to restore true feasibility. Two standard procedures enforce this elimination: * **The Big-M Method:** Penalizes the presence of artificial variables by assigning them an exceptionally large objective coefficient $M > 0$ (added as $+M \sum R_i$ in minimization or $-M \sum R_i$ in maximization), forcing them out of the basis during standard iterations. * **The Two-Phase Method:** Deconstructs the solution into two sequential linear programs. Phase I optimizes an auxiliary objective function minimizing the sum of all artificial variables ($\min w = \sum R_i$). If the optimal value of Phase I is $w^* = 0$, all artificial variables have left the basis; the artificial columns are discarded, and Phase II proceeds with the original objective function starting from the feasible basis found.
